Artist.value: Maison Méditerranéenne Des Sciences de l'Homme Phonothèque, André Raymond

ImageDescription.value: This church, which has been part of the architectural landscape of the city of Mosul since 1873, is also known as the Latin Church (al-kanîsah al-lâtiniyah) or the Church of the Clock (kanîsat al-sâ'ah) thanks to its bell tower with a clock with four dials. Empress Eugénie de Montijo, wife of Napoleon III, had financed the construction of the bell tower (the first in Iraq) built between 1881 and 1882. The complex included a church, a seminary with housing for communities of brothers and sisters, a boys' school, a girls' school, as well as a hospital and a house for missionaries. A school for teachers was later added. The Dominicans also installed a printing press there. The photo shows part of the complex, as well as the street on which it is located. It shows two cars, one white and one black, driving down the street in front of the complex, as well as a parked scooter with two men on it, and other people, men, walking alongside the building. On the slide holder A. Raymond has written "Dominicans."
